title: Choosing Aida fabric for cross-stitch
subtitle: Counts, colours, and what each does for the finished piece
excerpt: Aida is a woven cotton made specifically for counted cross-stitch. Its threads are grouped into a regular grid of holes. The count number tells you how many squares per inch: 14-count is the standard starting fabric; higher counts give finer detail. Colour choice is permanent, so pick it before cutting.
sourceNotes: Aida fabric counts and characteristics documented in standard cross-stitch references including Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Modern Aida specifications from manufacturer technical literature (Zweigart, 14-count = 28 threads per 10 cm).

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of Aida squares or evenweave thread pairs per inch of fabric. A higher count means smaller squares and finer stitches; a lower count means larger squares and chunkier stitches. 14-count Aida has 14 squares per inch and is the standard beginner fabric.

content.text: Aida is woven cotton with its threads grouped into a regular grid. Each group of threads defines one square; the corners of each square meet at a hole. The
tells you how many squares fit into one inch of fabric. A
occupies one square regardless of count; the count determines the physical size of that square.

The largest standard count. Each square is very visible and easy to work with a size 22 tapestry needle and three strands of floss. Good for children or anyone new to needlework who needs to see the grid clearly. The finished piece is proportionally larger than the same design on 14-count.

The standard count. Works with a size 24 tapestry needle and two strands of floss for the fill, one strand for the back-stitch outline. The finished piece is a practical size for most small and medium designs. Most beginner charts are designed for 14-count.

A moderately finer fabric. Two strands of floss still work at 16-count; the needle drops to size 26. The squares are smaller, so the same design worked at 16-count comes out about twelve per cent smaller than at 14-count.

Fine detail fabric. One strand or two very fine strands of floss; a size 28 tapestry needle. The squares are small enough that a magnifier is useful for most stitchers. Produces crisp, detailed work on smaller pieces.

Aida comes in white, antique white (cream), natural, ecru, and a full range of dyed colours. White gives the truest colour rendering: thread colours appear exactly as they look on the card. Cream or natural softens the background and reads warmer, which suits floral and botanical charts. Coloured Aida works when the chart is designed for it, most often for seasonal pieces where the background colour is part of the design.
The fabric colour is permanent once you begin stitching. Read the chart notes before cutting the fabric; some designers specify the background colour as part of the finished effect.

A standard rule: add at least five centimetres (two inches) on every side of the design area to allow for the hoop margin and the finishing margin. A design that measures 15 centimetres wide needs at least 25 centimetres of fabric. Oversize rather than under-size: Aida that is too narrow to fit the hoop cannot be extended.
